short: Speaker-conditioned video-to-speech with adversarial identity removal: both standard (gradient reversal on GRID lips dates from 2017); EER uses the training embedding network; one run.
position: The paper [@oneata2021speaker] changes the speaker input and its training (M03: an identity vector or frozen audio speaker embedding, plus an entropy or gradient-reversal speaker classifier stripping identity from the lip encoder) and the voice choice at inference (M08); both are standard. Its gradient-reversal variant is the device Wand and Schmidhuber put on a GRID lipreader in 2017 [@wand2017improving], absent from the paper's references, and Lip2Wav fed a speaker embedding to a lip-to-speech model a year earlier [@prajwal2020learning], which the paper calls "concurrent work" (Section II). The Abstract's "first" claim (voice control and unseen identities) therefore rests on adding identity removal, the feature the authors use to set Lip2Wav apart. The strongest confound: speaker control (EER) is scored with the embedding network that also feeds the SE models (Section IV.B). Seven of Table II's 18 speaker-conditioned rows (3-20) exceed baseline B's 41.9% unseen-speaker WER (inference), so "All these variants maintain or improve the content intelligibility" (Section V) is wrong.
